title: A service is one stored argv, and the installer that stores it is a sink
scope:
the `nvs service` namespace and what each verb does; the closed list of subcommands that may
be hosted; how an argv survives the Windows SCM's single-string `ImagePath`; the identity a service runs
as and where its output goes; which service-manager control messages map onto which existing Novis
operation; and why installing on Windows and generating a unit on Linux are deliberately not the same
gesture. Not in scope: what `nvs serve` does, which is [0017](0017.md) and
[0074](0074.md); the control socket's protocol and what `reload` means,
which stay [0078](0078.md); periodic work, which is
[0073](0073.md) and is not a service; and bundling a program into one file,
which stays [0048](0048.md) — § 6 here is the boundary that ADR's § 1
named and deferred.

summary.headline: A service install stores one command line, and the installer fails closed
summary.body:
Installing Novis as a service registers the binary with the platform's service manager and
stores the command line after `--` verbatim, so any option the binary accepts is available to a
service. Because a privileged account runs that line at every boot, the installer refuses
anything doubtful: only serving and running may be hosted, no relative paths, no install whose
output goes nowhere, no password on a command line. On Windows the service runs under a
per-service virtual account; on Linux the tool prints a hardened systemd unit and writing it is
an explicit opt-in.
